shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner at high altitude approaching its destination, in daylight and visual conditions. Thunderstorms near the destination meant aircraft were being held.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying and the captain the pilot monitoring. The captain had about 1,400 hours on type, 60 in the last 90 days; the first officer about 1,800 hours on type, 104 in the last 90 days.

What happened. Air traffic control assigned holding at a waypoint at flight level 370. The first officer built the hold in the flight management computer and the captain checked it. Approaching the hold, with vertical navigation engaged, the aircraft slowed from about Mach 0.75 to the calculated holding speed of 229 knots. Both pilots noted that this was close to the low-speed band at that altitude and identified it as a threat to watch. They were also checking the hold and working out fuel and holding time for a possible diversion. Approaching the fix, the controller cleared them to descend to flight level 360. The aircraft descended in vertical navigation mode while still slowing, and the thrust levers came back almost to idle. At level-off the autothrottle increased thrust slowly, and both pilots saw the aircraft sink about 100 ft below the new level as it crossed the fix and began a right turn into the hold. The first officer pushed the thrust levers forward and guarded the control column, but the engines spooled up slowly.
safe_outcome: TCAS then gave a traffic advisory, followed by a resolution advisory to climb, on an aircraft established in the hold 1,000 ft below. The crew responded, and the aircraft returned to its assigned level without coming closer to the other traffic. The aircraft continued to its destination without further incident. No one was hurt and no aircraft was damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Deviation D4 applies: the real event included a TCAS traffic advisory and a resolution advisory, so they are in the safe ending, and it ends 'No one was hurt and no aircraft was damaged.' Removed under rule 3: both pilots' debriefs (being caught off guard by the throttle reduction, 'distracted' by holding and fuel checks, RA training 'ingrained' for lower altitudes, the RA commanding a manoeuvre that would have made things worse, the roll creating the best escape path), the reason for raising the selected speed afterwards, the 'report has been submitted' line, and the synopsis wording. Kept as activity at the time, without the word 'distracted': the crew were checking the hold and working out fuel and holding time for a possible diversion. Moved under rule 5: the traffic 1,000 ft below (the crew learned of it only from the TCAS), the advisories, the crew's response, the stick shaker, the recovery and the continuation. Judgement calls for James: (1) the safe ending here contains crew actions (the response to the RA, a brief stick shaker and upset recovery) that the bad ending does not, so the two versions differ in more than the outcome. These could not go in the shared text, because they follow the advisory. James may want to trim the safe ending to the advisory and recovery, or drop the case; (2) the captain not reporting the RA on the busy frequency, and the reasons given for it in the debrief, are left out of the safe ending, because they are later decisions explained afterwards; (3) the 'yellow band' is rendered as 'the low-speed band'; the throttle indications (RETARD, then FMC SPD) are summarised as 'almost to idle'. Bracket: 'crossing', because the conflicting traffic was holding below, with this aircraft sinking and turning over it; neither climbing nor descending fits. | EDITED by Claude, 1 Oct (deviation D6): the safe ending was trimmed to the advisories and the outcome. The crew's response to the resolution advisory (the brief stick shaker and the upset recovery) was removed, because it added crew actions present in only one version.
